In summary, our research is concerned with
stimulus equivalence in children.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
matching-to-sample is a viable and effective procedure for establishing stimulus control in children.
the data support the notion that stimulus control can be established by matching to sample and that stimulus control is the basis of generative performance.
stimulus equivalence is an automatic and inevitable consequence of the establishment of stimulus relations, and is not a separate and independent phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the establishment of a stimulus equivalence class is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for the emergence of generative performances.
stimulus control is the primary determinant for the formation of equivalence classes and that equivalence classes are not necessary for the acquisition of generative performances.
the formation of equivalence classes in children can be accomplished without mediation of verbal behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that

matching to sample is a powerful tool for the formation of complex relations between stimuli and that the use of matching-to-sample procedures is an important step in the evolution of behavior analysis.
stimulus equivalence is a robust phenomenon in children, even when the training conditions do not include the verbal mediation of the stimuli.

the matching-to-sample procedure, which has been used in a variety of applied settings (e.g., teaching children to read and spell, teaching children with autism to label objects, teaching children to solve math problems, teaching children to identify colors, teaching children to name animals), is also a very useful procedure for the basic study of human learning.
